sections.title: Prerequisite: The Bernoulli Trial
sections.content: Define a Bernoulli trial as an experiment with exactly two outcomes: Success (S) or Failure (F). Emphasize that probability p must remain constant.
sections.example: Visual animation: A coin flip. Heads (p=0.5) vs Tails (1-p=0.5).

sections.title: Defining the Binomial Conditions (BINS)
sections.content: Introduce the BINS acronym: Binary (two outcomes), Independent trials, Number of trials is fixed, Success probability is constant.
sections.example: Animated checklist showing a squirrel gathering nuts: Is it a success if it finds one? Are the tries independent? Yes!

sections.title: The Binomial Formula
sections.content: Present the formula: P(X=k) = C(n, k) * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k). Explain that C(n, k) calculates the number of ways to arrange 'k' successes in 'n' attempts.
sections.example: Visual tree diagram showing 3 flips of a coin, highlighting how many paths lead to exactly 2 Heads.

sections.title: Application: The Robot Scout
sections.content: Walk through a practical scenario. A robot scout has a 70% chance of successfully identifying a mineral. If it scans 5 sites, what is the probability it finds exactly 4?
sections.example: Step-by-step calculation: n=5, k=4, p=0.7. Show the probability distribution curve shifting as we solve it.

sections.title: Summary & Visualization
sections.content: Reiterate that the distribution shape depends on 'n' and 'p'. Preview how this predicts real-world likelihoods.
sections.example: An animated histogram morphing shape as 'p' changes from 0.1 to 0.5 to 0.9.
